conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mrs. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your neurology team members. You're here today for your second dose of methotrexate for your primary CNS lymphoma. How have you been feeling since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been doing okay overall. I’ve been at the rehab center and working on my strength. But I’ve noticed this numbness and tingling in my right foot for about a week now. It feels like it’s fallen asleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is the numbness constant? Does it go up your leg at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started just in the foot, but over the last couple of days, the tingling has moved up a bit—now it’s going up the outside of my leg, maybe halfway to my thigh. It’s not severe, but it’s bothersome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting me know. Given your history of CNS lymphoma and MS, we want to make sure this isn’t related to nerve involvement from the cancer spreading. We’ll start with an ultrasound to rule out a blood clot, since you’re also on blood thinners for your DVT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I wasn’t sure if it was just my MS acting up again or something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point—MS can definitely cause these kinds of symptoms. But because of your lymphoma, we have to be extra cautious and rule out other causes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the results of your leg ultrasound. Good news—it shows no sign of a deep vein thrombosis. Your veins look normal with good blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s not a clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not a clot. But since the pain is moving up your leg, we’d like to do an MRI of your spine to make sure there’s no involvement of the spinal nerves by the lymphoma—specifically, we’re looking for something called leptomeningeal spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that common with my type of lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not common, but it can happen. The MRI will help us be sure. We’ll schedule it for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today you’ll be getting your second dose of methotrexate. We’ll give it through your PICC line, and you’ll also get leucovorin, sodium bicarbonate, and dexamethasone to protect your body from side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel different after the infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people tolerate it well. Some feel tired or have mild nausea, but we’ll monitor you closely. The dexamethasone also helps with brain swelling and might improve your energy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great with the methotrexate infusion. No complications so far. We’ll keep an eye on your labs over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m glad that’s done. Any update on the MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The spine MRI is back. I have good news—there’s no sign of lymphoma spreading to the spinal fluid or nerves. No leptomeningeal enhancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s such a relief. So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI did show some mild degenerative changes in your lower back, especially at L3-4, where there’s some narrowing near a nerve root. But it’s not pressing on anything. Given your history of MS, it’s possible this is a new flare of your MS affecting sensation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it could be MS, not the cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s actually the more likely explanation now that we’ve ruled out serious causes. We’d like to start you on gabapentin to help with the nerve pain and see if it improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve heard of that. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe and commonly used for neuropathic pain. We’ll start low and go slow to avoid dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I also want to talk about your liver tests. Your AST and ALT are elevated—higher than when you were last here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, yes. Methotrexate can affect the liver, and so can Keppra, which you’re on for seizure prevention. We’ve increased your leucovorin and IV fluids with sodium bicarbonate to help clear the methotrexate faster and protect your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we expect it will. We’ll keep monitoring, and you’ll take leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate by mouth for three more days after discharge. Your oncologist will check your liver enzymes in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed my dexamethasone was changed from twice a day to once a day. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s part of tapering down. You’ve been on it for a while, and we want to reduce side effects like high blood sugar or mood changes. Since your brain swelling is under control, we can safely lower the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And what about my stomach medicine? I saw we switched from omeprazole to ranitidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good catch. Ranitidine doesn’t interact with methotrexate like omeprazole can, so it’s safer during chemo. It still protects your stomach, especially since you’re on steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your methotrexate level has dropped to a safe range. That means your body is clearing it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. It means the leucovorin and hydration are working. Your liver numbers are still high, but we’ll keep following them as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling ready to go home. Will I need to come back soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in two weeks. That’s when you’ll get your third dose of methotrexate, and you’ll also have a port placed by interventional radiology for easier access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the port help with the infusions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’ll make things much smoother and reduce the need for repeated PICC lines. But you’ll need to hold your Lovenox injections the night before and the morning of that admission to reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I should keep taking the new gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice a day. If it helps, great. If not, your neurologist can adjust it. Also, keep taking your other meds like Advair, Singulair, and the calcium and vitamin D.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw on the discharge papers that they’re checking for hepatitis C. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s just a routine check. The result is pending, but if it’s positive, it’s important to know before continuing methotrexate, since it can affect the liver more in that case. We’ll follow up with your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Everything looks good for discharge. Your neurologic exam is stable, your vitals are normal, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve been looking forward to going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with prescriptions for gabapentin, ranitidine, and a few days of leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate. Stop the Dilaudid and omeprazole—we don’t need them anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll see the oncologist soon for the lab follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll call you about your liver tests. And we’ll see you back here in two weeks for the port and next chemo dose. Keep in touch with your husband and let us know if anything changes—like new weakness, severe pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well, and we’re here to support you. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.
